summary.text: Exhaustive trial-division searches supply Goldbach decompositions for every even integer from \(4\) through \(8012\) and Lemoine decompositions for every odd integer from \(7\) through \(15727\); above those thresholds, any counted representation directly gives \(n=(n-q)+q\) in the even case and \(n=(n-2q)+2q\) in the odd case, with both summands prime. For any bound \(N\), applying the hypothesis to the even number \(2N+8014\) yields \(2q<n\), so \(r=n-q-6>N\), while \(r\) and \(r+6=n-q\) are prime; hence cousin-prime pairs are unbounded and therefore infinite.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
c(n)=1+(n\bmod 2).
\]
Thus \(c(n)=1\) when \(n\) is even and \(c(n)=2\) when \(n\) is odd. By the definition of A219055, \(a(n)\) is the number of natural numbers \(q<n\) such that
\[
(c(n)+1)q<n,
\]
\(q\) and \(q+6\) are prime, and, on putting
\[
p=n-c(n)q,
\]
both \(p\) and \(p-6\) are prime. The inequality \((c(n)+1)q<n\) is exactly the condition \(p>q\), since \(p=n-c(n)q\).

Assume the core conjecture:

* if \(n>8012\) is even, then \(a(n)>0\);
* if \(n>15727\) is odd, then \(a(n)>0\).

We prove in turn Goldbach’s conjecture, Lemoine’s conjecture, and the infinitude of prime pairs differing by six.

## 1. The finite computations used below

For completeness, the cases below the two thresholds were settled by the following exhaustive calculation.

Primality was tested by trial division. For a natural number \(m\), the test proceeds as follows. Numbers below \(2\) are declared nonprime; \(2\) is declared prime; an even number greater than \(2\) is declared nonprime. For an odd number greater than \(2\), the odd integers
\[
3,5,7,\ldots
\]
are tested in succession until the next divisor \(d\) satisfies \(d^2>m\). The number is declared composite if one of the tested integers divides it, and prime otherwise.

This test is sound. Indeed, if an odd \(m>2\) is composite, its least prime divisor \(r\) satisfies \(r^2\le m\): writing \(m=rs\) with \(r\le s\) gives \(r^2\le rs=m\). Since \(m\) is odd, \(r\) is odd, so it occurs among the tested divisors. Conversely, finding a divisor between \(2\) and \(\sqrt m\) proves compositeness. Hence a number accepted by the test is prime.

For each integer \(n\), two finite searches were used:

1. the Goldbach search examines successive \(q\), beginning with \(q=2\), and succeeds when both \(q\) and \(n-q\) pass the primality test;
2. the Lemoine search examines successive \(q\), beginning with \(q=2\), and succeeds when both \(q\) and \(n-2q\) pass the primality test.

At most \(n\) successive candidates are examined in either search. If the first search succeeds, say at \(q\), then \(q\) and \(n-q\) are prime. In particular \(n-q\ge2\), so no issue involving truncated subtraction can occur, and
\[
n=(n-q)+q.
\]
Likewise, if the second search succeeds, then \(q\) and \(n-2q\) are prime, hence \(n-2q\ge2\), and
\[
n=(n-2q)+2q.
\]
Thus every reported success gives an actual decomposition of the desired kind.

The exhaustive calculation gave the following results:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{for every }0\le j<4005, &&4+2j\text{ has a successful Goldbach search};\\
&\text{for every }0\le j<7861, &&7+2j\text{ has a successful Lemoine search}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The Goldbach calculation was split into the index blocks
\[
[0,500),[500,1000),[1000,1500),[1500,2000),
\]
\[
[2000,2500),[2500,3000),[3000,3500),[3500,4000),[4000,4005),
\]
and the Lemoine calculation into
\[
[0,500),[500,1000),\ldots,[7000,7500),[7500,7861).
\]
In each block, every index was enumerated, the relevant candidates \(q\) were searched in order, and primality of the two summands was established by the trial-division test just described. These blocks cover their indicated index intervals without gaps.

The endpoint arithmetic is important. Every even \(n\) with \(4\le n\le8012\) can be written uniquely in the form
\[
n=4+2j
\]
with \(0\le j\le4004\), hence with \(j<4005\). Therefore the first calculation proves Goldbach decompositions for every even \(n\) in this entire range. Similarly, every odd \(n\) with \(7\le n\le15727\) can be written as
\[
n=7+2j
\]
with \(0\le j\le7860\), hence with \(j<7861\). Therefore the second calculation proves Lemoine decompositions for every odd \(n\) in that entire range.

## 2. What positivity of \(a(n)\) supplies

Suppose first that \(n\) is even and \(a(n)>0\). Since \(a(n)\) counts a finite set, positivity means that at least one member \(q\) of that set exists. Because \(n\) is even, \(c(n)=1\). Consequently this \(q\) satisfies
\[
2q<n,
\]
and all four numbers
\[
q,\qquad q+6,\qquad n-q,\qquad n-q-6
\]
are prime. In particular, if we put \(p=n-q\), then \(p,q,p-6,q+6\) are prime and \(n=p+q\). The identity is legitimate in the natural numbers because \(2q<n\) implies \(q<n\).

Suppose next that \(n\) is odd and \(a(n)>0\). Now \(c(n)=2\), so some \(q\) satisfies
\[
3q<n,
\]
and
\[
q,\qquad q+6,\qquad n-2q,\qquad n-2q-6
\]
are all prime. In particular, putting \(p=n-2q\), we have
\[
n=p+2q.
\]
Again, \(3q<n\) implies \(2q<n\), so the subtraction is genuine.

These two observations are the direct bridge between the assumed positivity statement and the two additive conjectures.

## 3. Goldbach’s conjecture

Let \(n\ge4\) be even. There are two cases.

If \(n\le8012\), the finite computation in Section 1 supplies primes \(p,q\) with
\[
n=p+q.
\]

If \(n>8012\), the core conjecture gives \(a(n)>0\). By the even extraction in Section 2, there is a prime \(q\) for which \(p=n-q\) is prime and \(2q<n\). Hence
\[
n=p+q.
\]

Thus every even integer \(n\ge4\) is a sum of two primes, which is Goldbach’s conjecture in the stated form.

## 4. Lemoine’s conjecture

Let \(n\ge7\) be odd. Again split into two cases.

If \(n\le15727\), the finite computation in Section 1 supplies primes \(p,q\) satisfying
\[
n=p+2q.
\]

If \(n>15727\), the core conjecture gives \(a(n)>0\). By the odd extraction in Section 2, there is a prime \(q\) such that \(p=n-2q\) is prime, and therefore
\[
n=p+2q.
\]

Thus every odd integer \(n\ge7\) is the sum of a prime and twice a prime, which is Lemoine’s conjecture in the stated form.

## 5. Infinitely many cousin-prime pairs

Let
\[
S=\{r\in\mathbb N:r\text{ is prime and }r+6\text{ is prime}\}.
\]
We prove that \(S\) is unbounded. Let \(N\) be an arbitrary natural number, and choose the even integer
\[
n=2N+8014.
\]
It is even and satisfies \(n>8012\). Hence the core conjecture gives \(a(n)>0\). By the even extraction, there is a \(q\) such that
\[
q,\ q+6,\ n-q,\ n-q-6
\]
are prime and
\[
2q<n.
\]
Define
\[
r=n-q-6.
\]
Then \(r\) is prime. Moreover,
\[
r+6=n-q,
\]
which is also prime. Thus \(r\in S\).

It remains to show that this member of \(S\) is larger than the prescribed bound \(N\). Since \(2q<n=2N+8014\), integrality gives
\[
q\le N+4006.
\]
Indeed, \(q\ge N+4007\) would imply \(2q\ge2N+8014=n\), contrary to \(2q<n\). Therefore
\[
r=2N+8014-q-6
  =2N+8008-q
  \ge 2N+8008-(N+4006)
  =N+4002>N.
\]
So for every natural number \(N\), there is an \(r>N\) such that both \(r\) and \(r+6\) are prime. Hence \(S\) is unbounded.

Finally, every finite subset of the natural numbers is bounded above (for example, by its maximum, with the empty set bounded trivially). Since \(S\) is unbounded, it cannot be finite. Thus there are infinitely many primes \(r\) for which \(r+6\) is also prime.

Combining Sections 3, 4, and 5, the core positivity conjecture for A219055 implies Goldbach’s conjecture, Lemoine’s conjecture, and the infinitude of cousin-prime pairs \((p,p+6)\), as required.
